https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/12/magy.text: Menü Kereső Magyar Péter: Balog Zoltán javasolta kitüntetésre Orbánnak Vásárhelyi Jánost, a bicskei gyermekotthon pedofíliáért elítélt volt igazgatóját Belföld frissítve Kersner Máté Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Balog Zoltán volt az a személy, aki Orbán Viktornál kitüntetésre javasolta Vásárhelyi Jánost, a bicskei gyermekotthon pedofíliáért elítélt egykori igazgatóját – posztolta ki Magyar Péter a Facebookon . A kötcsei piknikre érkező Orbán Viktort szombaton kora délután kérdezték az újságírók többek közt arról is , hogy miért terjesztette elő, hogy a bicskei gyerekotthon pedofil igazgatója állami kitüntetést kapjon. A volt miniszterelnök azt válaszolta, neki is felterjesztette valaki, így a sajtónak azt javasolta, hogy ezt az embert kérdezzék meg. Azt nem mondta el, ki volt a felterjesztő. Magyar Péter ezután posztolta ki a fenti bejegyzést, melyben megnevezte Balog Zoltánt. Telefonon kerestük Balog Zoltánt, de nem értük el, ezután írásban fordultunk hozzá. Ha választ kapunk a kérdéseinkre, beszámolunk róla. Magyar Péter szombat délelőtt Kátai-Németh Vilmos szociális- és családügyi miniszterrel és Gyurkó Szilvia gyermekjogi és gyermekvédelmi államtitkárral tartott sajtótájékoztatóján a Kossuth Lajos Gyermekotthonban bejelentette , hogy tízmilliárdos gyermekvédelmi krízisprogramot indít a kormány, és elkészült a kormány gyermekvédelmi jelentése . A tájékoztatón arról beszéltek: a rendszer az összeomlás szélén van. A miniszterelnök kiemelte, fontosnak tartja, hogy ne fordulhasson elő többé hasonló. „Titoktartás volt, ezeket fel fogjuk oldani” – mondta Magyar Péter, majd kivetített egy 2016-os kitüntetési javaslatot Orbán Viktor aláírásával, ebben Vásárhelyi Jánost, a bicskei gyerekotthon volt igazgatóját jelölte kitüntetésre a volt miniszterelnök. A kitüntetésről itt írtunk bővebben két éve. Magyar ezután K. Endréről és a bicskei gyerekotthonban elkövetett pedofil bűncselekményekről beszélt a sajtótájékoztatón. „Felfoghatatlan számomra magánemberként, és apaként, hogy minderről az Orbán-kormány tudott, és nem tett semmit” – mondta Magyar, aki szerint a jelentésekben benne voltak a most megjelentetett problémák is, mégsem történt semmi. Magyar ezután utalt arra, hogy Orbán Viktor a tavalyi kötcsei piknik után interjút adott az Öt.hu-nak , amelyben többek között arról beszélt, hogy a gyermekvédelmi rendszer lehetne jobb, de rendben van Magyarországon, majd beszélt arról is, hogy Tuzson Bence volt igazságügyi miniszter a Szőlő utcai ügyben kijelentette, „nincs kiskorú érintett”. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-lawma.text: BRUSSELS — European lawmakers are pushing to expand the EU’s flagship AI regulations to hold American tech companies liable for the risks their most advanced models pose to humanity, according to correspondence seen by POLITICO. The proposal by four senior lawmakers in the European Parliament would add new rules to the EU's landmark 2024 AI Act to ensure that companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic could be held liable when their technology is deployed in unforeseen ways. The move shows Brussels is waking up to a reality in which AI-powered harm is already happening, and risks are multiplying — and marks the first concrete effort within the EU to respond to fears over AI safety that are dominating the global political agenda. Advertisement Advertisement The group is calling on the Commission to introduce an AI Liability Act “to fill the legislative gaps currently existing for these kinds of incidents, so no people or European businesses are left empty-handed against these big providers when they cause harm," according to a Sept. 16 note to the Commission seen by POLITICO. Kim van Sparrentak, a Dutch Green Party member and part of the Parliament’s group monitoring the rollout of the bloc’s AI rules, said the fast-moving technology is forcing the EU to rapidly update what was two years ago the world's first major binding legislation to regulate advanced artificial intelligence models. “Europe needs to get ahead of the curve again,” said van Sparrentak, one of the four lawmakers leading the effort alongside German conservative Axel Voss, Italian Social Democrat Brando Benifei and Irish independent Michael McNamara. The call received support from lawmakers from the center-right European People's Party, the Socialists and Democrats group, and the liberal Renew group, indicating broad political backing. Extinction risks This week marks another major moment for global AI safety efforts, following a summer filled with AI hacking incidents and extinction-risk warnings. The topic will be top of mind at the U.N.'s General Assembly in New York, during a Tuesday meeting of G7 digital affairs ministers, and at a summit this week between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump. The EU lawmakers’ call draws attention to shortcomings in the AI Act that was agreed at a time when AI agents hacking other firms felt more like a sci-fi scenario. Advertisement Advertisement AI liability rules could make it easier and less costly for victims of AI-powered harm to claim compensation, for example, by shifting the burden of proof onto companies. A newfound focus on product liability in Europe would also jibe with some sentiment in the U.S. That included backing from former Trump AI czar David Sacks at the POLITICO Decoded Summit in D.C. last week. The EU legislators' suggestion to add new liability rules shows a drastic reversal of the bloc’s public stance in recent months. For weeks, Brussels had offered a single standard response to the flurry of AI-powered incidents, warnings by AI researchers and calls from tech executives to slow down AI development: the EU’s Artificial Intelligence Act is already there to avoid companies losing control of their models or agents. The new focus on liability is a tacit admission that the AI Act alone won’t cut it. But the push for new rules is also legislatively awkward. The EU just revised its entire regime governing how products comply with safety standards, in an update to the EU’s general product liability rules that is set to take effect on Dec. 9. Advertisement Advertisement Brussels is also on a quest to slash more tech regulation in an effort to "simplify" rules to help businesses grow. AI-specific liability rules were suggested by the European Commission in September 2022, but the Commission withdrew them last year. Legal protections The bloc’s existing regulation already includes a view of AI through the lens of product safety. It pushes companies to assess their AI models or applications and determine the risk they pose to the audience: unacceptable, high, limited, or minimal. But the law does little to address the damage done. The law also doesn’t cover AI models before they’re deployed, during training or testing, even though most hacks last summer were conducted by agents powered by internal-only research models. “The way it works right now basically grants no rights to people who are harmed by artificial intelligence,” said Mario Mariniello, senior fellow on digital and competition issues at think tank Bruegel. "It reduces the incentives for developers to factor in that risk and therefore invest into safety." Cybersecurity experts point to this summer’s incidents, such as the incident in which OpenAI-powered agents hacked into Hugging Face, as evidence of the need for a liability scheme. “I don’t think that it’s a good path to go on to say that because there was no criminal intent and the AI agent did it, there is no legal liability,” said Marcus Hutchins, a U.K. cyber expert who is best known for stopping a global outbreak of WannaCry software in 2017. Some experts, like associate professor Irene Kamara at Tilburg University, pointed to the fact that AI agents are often anthropomorphized, as if these are human-like protagonists launching an attack by their own: It "shifts the focus away from looking for the actual responsible individual(s) or persons behind the incident,” she said. https://business-review.eu/education/cal.text: BR EXCLUSIVE | Calbor College turns a former village school into an education campus rooted in community At Calbor College, education moves beyond the classroom and into the life of the village. Developed by Făgăraș Research Institute, the project brings students, researchers, craftspeople and local residents together in the former school of Calbor, a village in the Făgăraș region. A former village school in Calbor is gradually regaining its educational purpose. The building, which stopped operating as a school around 15 years ago and then stood unused for almost a decade, is being transformed by Institutul de Cercetare Făgăraș into a small educational campus. Its name, Calbor College, expresses the project’s central ambition: to continue the building’s history as a place of learning while creating space for students, researchers, teachers, children, craftspeople and members of the local community. Over the years, the building has served several public functions, including those of a school, boarding house and town hall. A renovation completed before the Institute took over the site removed many of its original features, including wooden windows, doors, stoves and other details that reflected its local architectural character. The Institute plans to recover some of these elements and recreate others using the original designs as references. Its team has also invested several years in addressing water infiltration and dampness, bringing the building closer to its future role as a fully functional educational campus. Read more about BR EXCLUSIVE | A former school in Saschiz becomes a shared home for NGOs, learning and local memory read more For Ștefan Cibian, president of Institutul de Cercetare Făgăraș, Calbor College represents a broader approach to education, one built around the relationship between learning, place and community. “Education, for us, belongs within the community. The building creates a powerful connection between the educational programmes we want to develop in Calbor and the local community,” Cibian says. This idea shapes the way the campus operates. Calbor College welcomes courses and visiting groups while also hosting activities initiated by local residents, including workshops focused on traditional crafts and community education. The village plays an active role in the learning process. Its people, buildings, local knowledge and social changes become part of the educational experience, giving participants direct access to the realities of rural life in the Făgăraș area. The Institute already organises several programmes in and around the building. These include the Făgăraș Summer School, stone monument restoration camps, educational visits and activities developed with partner organisations. During the past three years, the College has also welcomed university students attending a course on Romanian identity and the social and political dynamics of Central and Eastern Europe. Sessions take place inside the former school and throughout the village, connecting academic discussion with direct observation. “We are bringing together education, different generations and people of all ages, so they can learn in the middle of a community with a distinctive history and a strong contribution to make to these educational processes,” Cibian explains. Authenticity as an educational resource The project’s approach to restoration reflects the same philosophy. The Institute sees the authenticity of the building and the village as a source of knowledge, rather than a purely aesthetic quality. The building carries traces of several stages in Calbor’s history. Its architecture, former functions and relationship with local residents offer participants a way to understand how public spaces evolve alongside the communities that use them. “Authenticity speaks about what the Calbor community and the Făgăraș region have been, what they are today and what they can become. It is an essential part of high-quality education,” Cibian says. This authenticity includes the village’s current challenges and transformations. Students and visitors encounter changes in population, local livelihoods, crafts, property use and community structures. They also meet residents who continue local practices, restore buildings, develop initiatives and negotiate the future of the village through everyday decisions. BR EXCLUSIVE | How Transylvanian villages are reinventing places of learning The experience gives abstract subjects a physical and social context. Participants can examine regional history through houses and public buildings, cultural identity through local practices, and social change through conversations with the people living through it. “Being in the middle of a community with its own history and internal dynamics gives you an educational and cultural experience. Direct experience allows you to understand ideas that remain much harder to grasp through reading or discussion alone,” Cibian adds. The learning process also works in the opposite direction. The presence of young people, academics and visitors from Romania and other countries creates new exchanges for the local community. According to Cibian, these encounters can generate confidence, energy and learning opportunities for residents. They bring new people into the village, create occasions for collaboration and give local knowledge a visible role within wider academic and cultural conversations. A campus shaped by the village Calbor College is developing as an educational laboratory shaped by its surroundings. The former school provides the physical infrastructure, while much of the subject matter lies across the village, in its houses, monuments, crafts, family histories and changing social relationships. This model allows participants to study a community through sustained contact and shared activities. Restoration camps connect practical work with the history of local materials and construction techniques. University courses gain additional depth through conversations and field observation. Craft workshops give residents a direct role in transmitting knowledge. The project also gives a vacant public building a renewed function. Its educational purpose remains connected to its previous life as a village school, while its audience and curriculum extend far beyond the traditional classroom. The result is a campus whose walls belong to the former school and whose learning environment extends across the entire village.
